title: Disputed New Testament books said to wait on Church determination
source_text: XXVIII. Cum vero de quibusdam libris vere divinis & Apostolicis aliquando inter ipsos orthodoxos dubitatum sit, ut ex. gr. de Epistola ad Hebraeos, de Epistola Jacobi, de Epistola Judae, & posteriore Epistola Petri, & de secunda & tertia Joannis, ejusdemque Apocalypsi, id inde factum afferunt & pertendunt, quod Ecclesia de his libris judicium & sententiam suam nondum pronunciarat: istam vero dubitationem tandem per Ecclesiae determinationem & judicium sublatam fuisse. Nempe in Laodicena Synodo, & III. Carthaginiensi, Innocentiiique & Gelasii PP. decretis, quibus non tantum praedicti Novi Testamenti libri, sed illi quoque de quibus adhuc hodie lis est inter nos & Pontificios, An ad Veteris Testamenti Canonem pertineant, in Scripturae Canonem, ut quidem illi volunt, recepti sunt. Atque in hujus rei confirmationem afferunt etiam quod de Epistola Jacobi scribit Hieronymus, Et si ab alio quodam sub ejus nomine scripta afferebatur, tamen paulatim procedente tempore obtinuit authoritatem. Et quod de Epistola Judae similiter dicit, Quod, etsi a plerisque rejiciebatur, tamen authoritatem vetustate & usu meruit. Quibus consentanea sunt quae de Epistola quoque ad Hebraeos, & Joannis Apocalypsi scribit idem Hieronymus epistola ad Dardanum, Nos, inquit, utraque recipimus, nequaquam hujus temporis consuetudinem, sed, veterum Scriptorum authoritatem sequentes, qui plerumque utriusque utuntur testimoniis, non ut interdum de Apocryphis facere solent, sed quasi Canonicis & Ecclesiasticis.
pass_a_gloss: But when certain books truly divine and Apostolic were sometimes doubted even among the orthodox themselves — for example the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the Epistle of Jude, the later Epistle of Peter, and the second and third of John, and his Apocalypse — they assert and contend that this happened because the Church had not yet pronounced its judgment and sentence on these books; but that that doubt was at last removed by the Church's determination and judgment. Namely in the Synod of Laodicea, and the third of Carthage, and the decrees of Popes Innocent and Gelasius, by which not only the aforesaid New Testament books, but also those about which there is still today a dispute between us and the Pontificals — whether they belong to the Old Testament Canon — were received into the Canon of Scripture, as indeed they will have it. And for confirmation of this they also bring what Jerome writes about the Epistle of James: And although it was being put forward as written by someone else under his name, yet little by little as time went on it obtained authority. And what he says similarly about the Epistle of Jude: That although it was rejected by most, yet it earned authority by antiquity and use. Agreeing with which are what the same Jerome writes in the letter to Dardanus about the Epistle to the Hebrews also and John's Apocalypse: We, he says, receive both, following by no means the custom of this time but the authority of the ancient writers, who for the most part use the testimonies of both, not as they sometimes do with the Apocrypha, but as if with Canonical and Ecclesiastical books.
pass_b_english: When even among the orthodox some truly divine and Apostolic books were sometimes doubted — Hebrews, James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, and the Apocalypse — they claim this was because the Church had not yet given its judgment, and that the doubt was finally lifted by church determination: at Laodicea, the third council of Carthage, and the decrees of Popes Innocent and Gelasius.
By those, they say, not only the New Testament books just named, but also the Old Testament books still disputed between us and Rome, were received into the Canon — as they would have it.

For confirmation they cite Jerome on James: though it was being put about as written by someone else under his name, little by little it gained authority. On Jude: though most rejected it, antiquity and use earned it authority.

In the same vein Jerome writes to Dardanus on Hebrews and John's Apocalypse: We receive both, following not present custom but the authority of the ancient writers, who usually cite both not as they sometimes do the Apocrypha, but as Canonical and Ecclesiastical.

choices.why: Their claim about delayed church judgment.
